Paragraph:
Translation: The senses are so strong and impetuous, O Arjuna, that they forcibly carry away the mind even of a man of discrimination who is endeavoring to control them.

Purport (Excerpt): There are many learned sages, philosophers and transcendentalists who try to conquer the senses, but in spite of their endeavors, even the greatest of them sometimes fall victim to material sense enjoyment due to the agitated mind... Therefore, it is very difficult to control the mind and the senses without being fully Krsna conscious. Without engaging the mind in Krsna, one cannot cease such material engagements...
Situation/Problem_Faced: The terrifying realization that intellectual knowledge ('discrimination') and massive effort are often not enough to stop one from making terrible, self-destructive choices in the heat of the moment.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: Krishna validates the immense, forceful power of human impulses. He warns that the senses are so violent and turbulent that they can hijack the mind of even the most educated and disciplined individuals if they rely solely on their own strength.
Outcome/Resolution: Arjuna is warned against the arrogance of relying purely on intellect or sheer willpower to combat deeply rooted sensory drives.

Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.The Power of Impulses: The 'impetuous' nature of biological and psychological drives
Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.Ego and Vulnerability: Acknowledging that even a 'man of discrimination' can be forcibly overcome
Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.Addiction Relapse: Falling victim to destructive habits despite conscious 'endeavors' to control them

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Pramathini (Turbulent, violent, or agitating nature of the senses)
Indriyani balavanti (The overpowering strength of the senses)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: The text cites historical examples of great sages falling from grace because they relied on mechanical yoga and personal strength. The senses are fundamentally too powerful for the unprotected mind. True control is only possible by fully engaging the mind in the Supreme (Krishna consciousness), providing divine protection against sensory hijack.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: This verse normalizes the intense struggle of self-control. It highlights a critical psychological truth: knowledge is not behavior. You can know exactly what is right ('a man of discrimination') and still be forcibly carried away by anger, lust, or addiction because the neurological pathways of the senses are overwhelmingly strong. It warns against arrogance, emphasizing that successfully managing our impulses requires profound humility, vigilance, and anchoring the mind in something greater than our own fragile willpower.
